topics.title: Pattern overview
topics.summary: Let one object use different ways of doing the same task without embedding every algorithm in that object. The changing part is the calculation or policy; the surrounding workflow should remain stable when another supported method is added.

blocks.title: Learning objectives
items: Separate a stable workflow from a replaceable calculation.
Trace a virtual call and a transfer of ownership.
Add a calculation while preserving validation and existing behavior.

blocks.text: The context holds an object through a shared strategy interface. The client chooses a concrete strategy and supplies it to the context. When work arrives, the context calls that interface rather than testing every algorithm name. Replacing the installed object changes the chosen algorithm without replacing the context. This is composition: one object performs part of its job by using another object.

cards.question: What problem does Strategy address?
cards.answer: Let one object use different ways of doing the same task without embedding every algorithm in that object. The changing part is the calculation or policy; the surrounding workflow should remain stable when another supported method is added.

cards.question: What is Strategy?
cards.answer: A replaceable object or callable that supplies one way to perform a task.

cards.question: What is Context?
cards.answer: The object that keeps stable work and calls a selected strategy.

cards.question: What is Precondition?
cards.answer: A rule that must already hold when an operation begins.

cards.question: Must Strategy use inheritance and heap allocation?
cards.answer: No. A callable or function pointer can express a simple interchangeable algorithm. This class-based version makes roles explicit and supports independently implemented strategy objects.

cards.question: Which class decides whether an empty batch is allowed here?
cards.answer: Monitor enforces the shared input boundary before delegation. Its strategy implementations rely on that stated contract when called through Monitor.

topics.title: One screen, two useful readings
topics.summary: A room monitor receives a small batch of whole-number readings. Each reading is from 0 through 1000. A batch contains 1 through 1000 readings. The ordinary screen shows the average, rounded down. During a review, an operator wants the highest reading instead. Both views use the same batch. Neither view may edit the stored readings. The input limits keep arithmetic predictable and make a missing batch an error rather than a made-up zero.

topics.title: The specific limit: unrelated changes share one function
topics.summary: Now a third team wants the middle reading after sorting. A fourth wants a calibrated result with stored settings. Each addition changes the same selection function. A new branch can accidentally skip shared validation. Sorting the original batch to find the middle also changes data that another screen expected to keep in arrival order. These are concrete costs, not proof that every if statement is bad.

blocks.text: We need a small interchangeable rule, called a strategy. The monitor keeps the stable work: check inputs, then ask its current rule for one answer. Each rule owns its calculation. The caller chooses the rule because the caller knows what the operator requested. This arrangement is the Strategy pattern. Its purpose is replaceable behavior. The number of classes is a consequence of that need, not the goal.

topics.title: A contract larger than a function signature
topics.summary: Estimate declares value. The const reference borrows a vector and forbids changing its elements through that reference. The final const describes the Estimate object used for the call: value promises not to change its ordinary members. These are two separate const promises. The function returns a new integer value, so its result does not borrow storage from the vector.

blocks.text: The interface also has a written contract. Its caller supplies a nonempty validated batch, and the rule returns a whole-number estimate without changing that batch. Average and Highest rely on that precondition. Calling either concrete rule directly with an empty vector violates the contract: Average divides by zero; Highest would dereference an end iterator. The monitor is the intended public entry point for untrusted data. An interface does not cause the compiler to check these meaning-level rules.

Average uses integer division. With 1, 2, and 9, the sum is 12 and the answer is 4. With 1 and 2, the answer is 1. This is deliberate downward rounding for nonnegative values. At the largest accepted batch, the sum is at most 1,000,000, which fits the required ordinary int implementations with at least 32 bits. If the environment had only a 16-bit int, this chapter's arithmetic requirements would need a wider type. Highest uses max_element, which returns an iterator pointing at the largest element; the leading star reads the pointed-to integer.

topics.title: What the compiler fixes and execution selects
topics.summary: During compilation, the compiler checks the override signatures and that Estimate has the requested operation. A virtual call through rule_ selects the implementation belonging to the actual object during execution. Replacing Average with Highest changes the selected object, not the code of Monitor::read. A compiler may optimize a call whose target it can prove, but the program must keep the same observable behavior.

blocks.text: A unique_ptr is the sole owning handle. Monitor receives that handle by value and moves it into rule_. std::move permits ownership transfer; it does not call the estimate or copy its readings. The arrow in rule_->value reaches the object owned by the handle and calls its method. On replacement, the previous strategy is destroyed. Monitor explicitly deletes copying; those user-declared copy operations also suppress its implicit move operations. The monitor itself therefore keeps a stable identity, while its strategy can be replaced. This avoids leaving a moved-from monitor with an empty rule. The virtual destructor makes destruction through the base type reach the complete derived object. Data is borrowed only for the duration of read; ownership of the strategy lasts until replacement or monitor destruction.

topics.title: Failure boundaries and a smaller alternative
topics.summary: select checks the proposed handle before assigning it. A null request throws, while the old strategy remains usable. read validates every reading before calling the strategy. These boundaries make failure local: a bad sample cannot partly sort or partly accumulate shared state inside the strategy. The current calculations themselves have no external effects. A future rule that writes a file would need a stronger contract about partial failure.

blocks.text: For a single stateless operation, a function pointer, a lambda, or std::function can express Strategy with less class code. A template parameter is attractive when the rule is fixed at compilation and speed or inlining matters. The virtual interface earns its place when selection occurs during execution, rule objects hold settings, or several operations belong to one rule. Do not add a strategy for each constant. A named parameter can represent a threshold without creating a new type.

In a long-lived monitor, replacement also raises a timing question: can one thread replace a rule while another calls read? This example is single-threaded and makes no such guarantee. A mutex, immutable shared snapshot, or an event-loop rule could define a safe policy. Merely using a smart pointer does not synchronize access to the member that holds it.

topics.title: Worked example: contracts and alternatives
topics.summary: A monitor with average and highest rules

blocks.title: Requirements
items: Accept 1–1000 integer readings, each from 0 through 1000.
Choose average or highest during execution; reject a missing strategy.
Keep input unchanged and keep the previous strategy after a rejected replacement.

blocks.text: Monitor centralizes validation while Estimate isolates the changing calculation. Owning the selected rule avoids a caller-lifetime dependency and permits replacement after construction.

blocks.title: Invariants
items: Every constructed Monitor owns a non-null strategy.
Every strategy call receives a nonempty bounded batch.
read does not change input; a rejected select leaves the old rule installed.

blocks.text: Alternative: A switch plus two free functions is easier for a permanently small choice set. A callable is also sufficient for stateless rules. The object interface becomes useful as policies gain settings or are supplied through a common runtime API.

Verification: main checks both calculations, singleton batches at 0 and 1000, empty input, a negative sample, and null replacement while retaining Highest. These checks are meaningful examples, not exhaustive proof over all bounded batches or concurrent access.

Maintenance: A new rule can be reviewed and tested independently of monitor validation. Keep the written preconditions next to the interface so future implementers do not silently add incompatible meanings.

topics.title: Exercise 20.6: Justify a decision
topics.summary: A reviewer proposes borrowing Estimate& inside Monitor to avoid heap allocation. Give a reasoned approval condition and a reasoned rejection condition.

blocks.title: Hint
blocks.text: Ownership is about who must keep an object alive.

blocks.title: Explained answer
blocks.text: Approve when the caller clearly outlives every monitor use and replacement can be represented safely, for example by a reference_wrapper. Reject a reference to a local strategy returned from a setup function: it would dangle. A good explanation states the lifetime contract and the allocation tradeoff; simply saying references are faster is insufficient.

workshop.title: A monitor with average and highest rules
workshop.problem: A monitor with average and highest rules. Accept 1–1000 integer readings, each from 0 through 1000. Choose average or highest during execution; reject a missing strategy. Keep input unchanged and keep the previous strategy after a rejected replacement.
workshop.output:
average=4
highest=9
empty, range, and null rejected

steps.why: Construction transfers the Average owner into the monitor.
read validates first; Average divides after adding.
select replaces the rule, then the same read method delegates again.
The null check runs before member assignment.

workshop.pitfall: Assign a null handle before checking it. The next read attempts to call through a null pointer, producing undefined behavior. The object no longer meets its non-null invariant.

discussion.question: A command-line tool has one fixed average calculation and exits after one batch. A live application accepts independently configured calculation objects. Choose a free function, template, or virtual Strategy for each and explain the deciding fact.
discussion.answer: Use a free function for the one fixed calculation. The live application can justify virtual Strategy because it receives objects during execution. A template is reasonable if the live application actually fixes each rule at compilation and never swaps it; selection time, not application size, decides.
discussion.hint: Ask when the rule must be selected and whether it has identity or settings.

workshop.alternative: A switch plus two free functions is easier for a permanently small choice set. A callable is also sufficient for stateless rules. The object interface becomes useful as policies gain settings or are supplied through a common runtime API.
workshop.design: Monitor centralizes validation while Estimate isolates the changing calculation. Owning the selected rule avoids a caller-lifetime dependency and permits replacement after construction.
invariants: Every constructed Monitor owns a non-null strategy.
Every strategy call receives a nonempty bounded batch.
read does not change input; a rejected select leaves the old rule installed.
workshop.maintenance: A new rule can be reviewed and tested independently of monitor validation. Keep the written preconditions next to the interface so future implementers do not silently add incompatible meanings.
workshop.verification: main checks both calculations, singleton batches at 0 and 1000, empty input, a negative sample, and null replacement while retaining Highest. These checks are meaningful examples, not exhaustive proof over all bounded batches or concurrent access.

lab.task: Add Middle as an Estimate implementation. Select it after the existing checks. Do not change Monitor or the original batch. Preserve every starter check and append the new deterministic output line shown by the solution.
lab.answer: Middle sorts a value copy, so its work cannot reorder the caller’s vector. It checks parity before indexing the lower middle element. A selection algorithm can reduce sorting work for large inputs, but the copied-and-sorted version is clearer at this chapter’s scale and satisfies the same contract.

overview.title: Strategy: a context owns its selected algorithm
overview.explanation: The ownership arrow runs from Monitor to its owned Estimate object. Inheritance arrows run from each concrete rule toward Estimate. They do not show execution order. Teaching comments describe responsibilities; they are not extra program members. At execution, Monitor validates the batch and calls the one installed object.
